I respectfully submit that, in view of these statements, it is the duty of the government not to undertake to solve the fast line question or make any change concerning the eastern phase of the transportation question before fully weighing these facts, which I have the honour of submitting, and which are confirmed in every respect by the reports of the two select committees of this House appointed to investigate the matter. This is not an attempt on my part to raise a cry against the ports of St. John or Halifax, but it is well known that these ports, by our present system of communication over Canadian territory and our government road, cannot compete with the short lines to Portland and to St. John through the state of Maine.
There is another portion of the evidence I would like to submit before resuming my seat, and this is evidence which has been forwarded me through the courtesy of the senior member for Cape Breton.
We all know that during the last five years the steamer Bruce has kept up a line of communication from Cape Breton to Newfoundland during the whole winter. I inquired from Captain Delaney, the commander of that steamer, what are the conditions in the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Bale de Cha-leur, to see if it was possible for a steamer to reach Paspebiac during December and January without meeting any ice. Here is his answer :
I have been making tri-weekly trips between Port-aux-Basques, Newfoundland, and North Sydney for the last five winters, and I have not seen any Ice before the latter part of February and the beginning of March, during that period, which would lead me to believe that ships could run to Paspebiac up to the end of January.
We have been told that North Sydney is the closest port to Europe and that Louisbourg is a great competitor for that honour, but if we take into consideration the combined rail and water route yon will see that Paspebiac can beat both of them.' You can reach it from Montreal after covering 539 miles of rail, and you cannot reach North Sydney without going over 989 miles of rail. I consider that we should utilize our water communication as much as possible tvhen available in preference to our railways, in order to reduce the rates of freight and exploit most effectively our natural advantages. In order to reach Cape Sydney or Louisbourg, you have to cover 400 miles more of rail than to reach Paspebiac. Our attempt to make Halifax .a national port has practically failed because the hulk of our exports go to St. John, and we all know that to reach St. John they have to go. not only over the Intercolonial Railway, but through American territory by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Between this and next session, the government may be in a position to submit a well defined scheme on this most vital question, and I would urge them to take into consideration this fact that the Bale de Chaleur is free from obstacles, that it is situated nearer the great centres of population of this country than any other portion of our waters after the closing of the St. Lawrence, and let me say that if the St. Lawrence could be utilized after the 25th of November, I would not ask that we should convey our passengers and freights to the Baie de Chaleur.
But, the St. Lawrence being closed, why cannot we use this beautiful expanse*of water as long as it can be utilized and then if any difficulties arise because of ice, there is no reason why the Intercolonial Railway trains should be switched off on the Atlantic and Lake Superior to Paspebiac ; they can go on to Halifax or St. John. I have submitted these facts for the consideration of

hon. members of this House and for the consideration of the government. I have done so in the interest of the people I represent, who, I belieVe, have been the victims of another injustice added to the long series of injustices inflicted upon them during the last fifteen or twenty years. But beyond fulfilling my duty to my own county and to the neighbouring county of Gaspd, in which I take a great deal of interest, and which is so worthily represented in this House by my learned colleague (Mr. Lemieux), I have come to the conclusion that the Baie de Chaleur not only offers advantages for prolonged local traffic but is the natural outlet of the great national highway to Europe. Paspebiac is, beyond doubt, as the facts demonstrate, on the shortest route to Europe. I believe that for the solution of the eastern phase of the great question of transportation we should go back to the Baie de Chaleur, which has been so neglected by all governments, and the we shall find in it the solution of our winter port and difficulties. We may find there what Jacques Cartier found when he first came to this country, for it was in the Baie de Chaleur that Jacques Cartier first discovered this beautiful land ; we may find there the solution of the problem before us as he found the solution of the great enterprise he had undertaken.

I shall not add anything to the very able argument presented by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) with regard to this question. I wish only to say a few words with regard to winter navigation along the shores of Gaspg and our railway communications. I share his views as to the possibilities of Paspebiac becoming the terminus of a fast line between Canada and Europe. But I beg to differ with him as to the best harbour in the counties of Gaspd and Bonaventure. I believe that Paspebiac is a fine harbour, with excellent facilities and splendid possibilities. But it has been recognized beyond the shadow of a doubt that the best harbour on the coast is in the county of Gaspe, and it is called Gaspd Basin. Indeed, my hon. friend has made a very able argument and I must congratulate him. He began by speaking of the steamer service which has existed for twenty or twenty-five years between Dal-housie in New Brunswick, and Gaspe Basin. Last winter, I know, there was a certain agitation in our respective counties with a view to improve that service. I may say at once, that the old [DOT] Admiral,' has been a faithful servant of the coast of Gaspe. But, at the same time I must admit she is too old to continue the service. As my hon. friend says, the line needs some improvement. I hear that the directors of the North American Transportation Company intend crossing the ocean this summer and getting a fine iron-built screw steamer, which is ex-Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure).
pected to begin semi-weekly trips by the beginning of next October. '
Last winter I was assailed with petitions and resolutions asking for all-winter navigation in the Bay of Gaspe and the Baie des Chaleurs. Whilst I am a believer in winter navigation in some degree, I do not share the optimism of my hon. friend as to continuous winter navigation in the Baie des Chaleurs or the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Though some reports may have been made by captains and commanders to the effect that navigation could be carried on the Whole year around, yet I have often conversed with some good old sea captains and navigators of my county, men who have spent their lives in navigating the waters of the Baie des Chaleurs and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Most of them speaking as honest men and experienced sailors, agreed in saying that while navigation was possible in the months of December and January, yet, during February and March it was almost impracticable. I say it again, I have the testimony of old sailors born and bred on the coast, men who have navigated these waters all their lives, who have been officers of the Marine and Fisheries Department, who have made a special study of the tides and currents, the winds and the movements of the ice in the Baie de Chaleur and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and they tell me that all-winter navigation is not feasible. Against such testimony, it is not sufficient to offer statistics and reports. So I would not advocate before this House a project based upon the idea of navigating those waters during the whole winter. As I said a minute ago, I have consulted some authorities on this subject, and I have summed up their opinions on the movement of ice in the Gulf of St. Lawrence in the following lines :	The
temperature on the coast of Gaspe is milder than the rest of the province of Quebec. Fresh water will freeze at 30 degrees above zero. Salt water "will not freeze above zero. During the severest winter the temperature will not go below zero except for eight or ten days. Therefore there is practically no ice in the salt water. The ice found in these waters is fresh water ice, which is formed in and is carried down by the St. Lawrence and other rivers emptying into the gulf. When this ice strikes Anticosti island it is met by a branch of the Arctic current, and is deflected towards the south. This deviation of the current, helped by the northern and western winds, which generally prevail in that region, causes the ice to accumulate in the straits of Northumberland and adjacent waters. The prevailing western winds cause the sea generally to be free of ice along the coast of the county of Gaspe. There is not much of that ice before the 1st or 15th of February ; and although the month of March is very mild, the ice remains until it is washed away in

April. The sea is free of ice in December and January, and navigation along the coast is possible until the 1st of February, and can be resumed on the 15th of April at the latest. Last winter the temperature was exceptionally mild, and there was no ice in the gulf ; there being no ice a steamer could have run between Dal-liousie and Gaspe. In conclusion, during the winter months, navigation is feasible between the 1st or 15th of April, at the latest, until the 1st of February in the following year. Perhaps it would be possible for vessels to resist the ice from the 1st of February to the 15th of April, but such vessels should be built as the ' Stanley, which, until lately was running between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, but such vessels are very costly.
Now, Sir, there was, last winter an agitation in my county in favour of a winter steam service. But last winter was an exceptionally mild one, there was no ice, and the same circumstances might not exist another year. We can have, as my hon. friend from Bonaventure has said, a steamer service between the 1st or 15th of April, until the 1st of February, or at least the 15th of January. As I stated it a moment ago, the ' Admiral ' is an old steamer, and although she has rendered very good service to the coast, a change is needed. My hon. friend and myself, have urged upon the government to induce the North American Transportation Company to put an iron screw steamer on the route, and I am glad to learn that by the 1st of October next, this new steamer will be ready to start, thereby rendering certain navigation during ten months; an event which the people along the coast will hail with satisfaction.
I might also mention another scheme that has been discussed in the county in connection with this question. Some people wanted a steamer service between the terminus of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway at New Carlisle, and GaspS Basin, instead of between Dalliousie and Gaspe Basin. I have objected strenuously to such a change, and my reason for doing so is obvious. The county of Gaspe and a part of the county of Bonaventure get their freight from Toronto, Montreal and Quebec. Now take a barrel of flour coming from Toronto, Montreal or Quebec ; it would be placed, say on board the cars of the Intercolonial Railway at Levis, would have to pay freight to the Intercolonial Railway, then to the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway, and it would have also to pay tribute to the steamer running between New Carlisle and Gaspe Basin. You can readily understand, Mr. Speaker, to what would amount our freight rates if such conditions existed, and I was justified in objecting to such a change. I am pleased to state that the Department of Trade and Commerce did not yield to the suggestions evidently made by the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company. Now,
Sir, if as 1 expect, we have a good iron screw steamer put on the route next October, the coast of Gasp6 will be satisfied provided the terminus is not changed.
As regards our railway communication, 1 fully agree with my hon. friend that the action of the Railway Committee of the Senate this morning was most deplorable. I regret to state that after our Bill had received the support of the Prime Minister, of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and of the Minister of Justice, and the unanimous assent of this House, the leader of the government in the Senate, the hon. the Secretary of State, saw fit to throw in his lot with those who for a quarter of a century have opposed the legitimate aspirations of the counties of Bonaventure and GaspS. I cannot understand how the leader of the government in the Senate found his way to vote against a Bill which had been to some extent, drafted by some of his colleagues. Yes, Sir, my hon. friend from Bonaventure and myself submitted the amendments agreed to by the interested parties, to the Minister of Justice, and to the Minister of Railways and Canals ; the amendments to the Bill were in fact drafted by them. How does it happen that the leader of the government in the Senate found his way to vote against that Bill ? Sir, I repeat that the Bill as amended, after having been sanctioned by the Minister of Justice, by, the Minister of Railways and Canals and by the Prime Minister himself, should have been, to say the least, given fair play by the Secretary of State. As I have already stated in this House, my hon. friend from Bonaventure and myself opposed the Bill as at first introduced, because we found in it no protection for the interests of the people we represent. But when these amendments had been accepted by the Prime Minister and his colleagues In this House, it was the duty of the Secretary of State to support the Bill and not nullify our common efforts as he did by his vote. I regret his action, and I desire to say that next year we shall make another attempt to get justice, not only from the government side but from the other side of the House as well.

I have listened with much Interest, and I have no doubt the House has also listened with much interest, to the remarks of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). It is apparent from the remarks of his colleague from Gaspg (Mr. Lemieux) that this is a question which has two sides to it, and I may be pardoned if I decline to express an opinion when two gentlemen having far superior opportunities of understanding the situation than I can boast of, have hitherto failed to agree. With respect, however, to the matters more particularly belonging to my own department, l will just say that I have carefully considered the request made by niy hon. friend from

i
Bonaventure and Gaspe, and the government will endeavour to supply as good a service as they possibly can obtain for the benefit of the inhabitants of those two counties. 1 believe that up to date the steamer * Admiral,' which has been engaged for a good many years, has rendered a very efficient service. But 1 am.aware that there are difficulties connected with the employment of paddlewheel steamers, and it may be necessary to substitute another. I am in correspondence with the company on that subject at present, and I hope to be able to meet the views of my hon. friends.

SMALL-POX OX SCHOONER ' JEANIE MYRTLE '-FISHERY AWARD- COASTING TRADE.
speechtext:
IvAULBACH (Lunenburg). Mr. Speaker, I take advantage of this opportunity to bring to the notice of the government a matter of very vital importance to every citizen of this Dominion, especially those residing near the sea engaged in shipping, but more particularly the sick seamen whose life as a rule is a hard one, when away from home and friends, and stricken down with dread disease. It will be remembered the Halifax newspapers on the 5th inst., reported the La Have schooner, ' Jeanie Myrtle,' Creaser, master, having entered i;he port of Hailfax from sea the day previous, with a sick seaman on board, and reported the same to the customs a hour after the port physician visited the ship, and when viewing the patient, at a glance pronounced it small-pox. The doctor was doubtful as to the case coming under the jurisdiction of the Dominion, but, as a precautionary measure ordered the yellow flag to be hoisted, and required the crew to remain by the vessel. When reaching the shore he wired the facts to the Minister of Agriculture, and asked for instructions, receiving as an answer, that the case was one for the local authorities, and as a result, the port physician acting under orders from here-Ottawa -refused to take any action beyond the precautions I have described.
The city authorities were next interviewed, and the chairman of the Board of Health of Halifax was asked about it, when the following episode, as reported, ensued
' What are you doing about the small-pox schooner ?'
' SVe have nothing to do with it.'
' Who has ?'
' I don't know, but not Halifax. The Ottawa telegram says " local authorities," but Or. Gil-p'c, on behalf of province, says "it's a county charge
* Are you going to allow the schooner to remain there a menace to the health of the community ?'
* The people on board have been told to stay there, and in the morning we will order the schooner to sea.'
' Where will she go ?'
' To LaHave, where she belongs, I suppose. When ordered from Canso she should have gone Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
straight home, and not put in here at all. Why should Halifax be saddled with the schooner that lies anchored over there near the Dart- * mouth shore ? '
' How can you order the vessel out of the harbour if you have no jurisdiction in the case?' the ' Herald ' asked.
But at this stage the conversation with Dr. Chisholm ended, for the genial chairman of the board of health declined to continue It.
A telegram was sent to me also the same day, which reads as follows :-
Halifax, N.S., May 5, 1902.
Schooner * Jeanie Myrtle,' Creaser, master, Ritcey's Cove, here with case of small-pox. Authorities refuse allow man land here. Has paid sick mariners' dues. Bad weather may detain vessel here days, with no attendance for man. See Minister Agriculture, ask him instruct Dominion physician to act.
BLACK, BROAD & CO.
This telegram was acted upon by me in the most energetic manner, by my calling first on the Minister of Agriculture, who informed me that he had a telegram from Halifax also, but was powerless to act at it was clearly provincial, and had answered in that way. I next applied to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and had the satisfaction of his telling me, after some slight inquiry and conference with his friends, that he would wire the officer of customs tor the port of Halifax to attend to the matter, though in reality it was no part, of the requirements of ins department, but that his action was purely from a motive of sympathy, under the peculiar circumstances of the case. I would say here, that both the Minister of Agriculture and Minister of Marine acted promptly in the matter, and X have no cause for complaint as respects either of them in that connection.
But I do say, and here state, that there is something radically wrong in this connection, that the Dominion, provincial and civic health authorities-all three should decline to act in this case, or care for this sick seaman, as a duty on their part. The very fact of the Dominion government receiving a sick mariner's fee, should in justice entitle a sick mariner having contagious disease to admission into the nearest contagious hospital that offered, and there cared for, with the best attendance possible, come from whence the patient may, within the province or from without. The expression of the chairman of the Halifax Board of Health, in the cold-hearted words, as referred to, ' In the morning we will send the vessel to sea,' if correct as reported, and I have no reason to doubt it, was very uncalled for, but in justice to him would say, that he must have given such utterance in an unguarded moment.
What is the object in exacting the sick mariner's due, I would ask, if it is not to give the sick seamen that comfort, and medical aid necessary to lead to his speedy recovery, and in the dread disease of small-

pox I contend the greatest effort should be exercised In the care of such patients, that they be kept isolated to prevent a spread, which can only he accomplished successfully in a regularly established contagious hospital, with a proper staff of attendants, that the patients may receive all necessary medical aid, care and attention.
I claim in all sincerity that the federal government should take this matter promptly in hand, and make such arrangemeuts and regulations as to settle this difficulty for ever, and have it clearly understood in future, that all sick seamen with contagious disease are to be received into the nearest contagious hospital and cared for at the expense of the federal government. This is most essential, and I sincerely hope the right hon. the First Minister will see that prompt action is taken with the view of better attention being given to this class of seamen.
Whilst I am on my feet I would ask the indulgence of the House to bring to its notice the subject of the fishery bounty. I may say that I greatly regretted my absence from the House (which was unavoidable owing to my having a cold) when the hon. member for Hamilton called attention to the statement of Premier Peters in the legislature of Prince Edward Island that ' there was no need of levying additional taxes to meet the prospective expenditure, because he was certain the Dominion government would pay over to the island government $1,000,000'as the island's share of the Halifax fishery awards.' It is also currently reported that approaches have been made by New Brunswick with the same object in view. The right hon. leader in reply stated that ' there was no ground for apprehension of this sort.' But I did not approve of his utterance that 1 It would make no difference whether this fund was administered by the Dominion or provincial authorities for the benefit of the fishermen.' I take serious exception to this, and in my mind it would make a very great deal of difference, were there to be no apportionment of this fund to the respective provinces, they to dispose of the fund as they thought proper, as the other province, Nova Scotia not excepted, would have the same view as to the appropriation as the island province expressed, and the matter of bounty for the encouragement of the fishermen would be a thing of the past. These governments have proved themselves in the past to be by no means, in the sense of the term parsimonious and would, were this money given them, spend it in an improvident manner, and the poor fishermen would in a short time have nothing in the way of bounty whatever:
The Question of the division of the fishery7 award, and the payment even of apportionments to the respective provinces, should not be entertained by7 this government for one moment, as the Dominion government is the most suitable body to be the trustee of such a fund, and not the provinces, a?
they would use the money to pay their provincial current expenses, and the bounty would be lost for ever. I here, in the most emphatic manner, protest against any attempt being made to take this fund out of the hands of the Dominion government, they being the most suitable trustees, or custodians of the fund, where we can feel assured it is safe from any attempt to have it utilized for any other purpose than that for which it was intended, viz., bounty for fishermen, it having been paid for the sacrifices the fishermen underwent, when the maritime fishing grounds were used by the United States fishermen in common with Canadian fishermen. The fishermen of the maritime provinces have a hard struggle at present to move along successfully even with the benefit of the bounty, as they7 have to compete with the bounty fed French fish of St. Pierre which means about $2 of a bonus on every7 quintal of French fish exported outside of France, Canada being excluded in the sale of fish to any French dependency, Guadeloupe and Martinique included. by reason of their prohibitory tariff. The French have the trade of these islands practically7 to themselves, and at the same time come into competition with us, with their bounty fed fish in the other markets of the world, the British West Indies included.
There is another matter of very great importance that I desire the First Minister to take cognizance of, and that is the coastwise trade of the West India Islands, enjoyed by British shipping from time immemorial, but now greatly interfered with by the embargo set up by the United States since their acquirement of the island of Porto Rico, and the monopoly of that market, which up to a recent date was largely7 the market for Nova Scotia fish, in fact the very best of all the West India group. Of course I am aware that we cannot now control this matter, but it might have been managed satisfactorily to us had active measures been taken by this government, and I strongly advised to have the imperial government informed of our interest and trade with this island, and to induce Great Britain to demand an undertaking from the United States government that they would not be allowed to plant their flag on that island-Porto Rico-inhabited by a law-abiding and peaceful people, unless they7 consented to allow the same privileges for trading with them, in common with the United States, that we previously enioyed. I tried to impress this government with the importance of the Porto Rico trade to Nova Scotia, and pointed out how essential it was in our interest to have them take prompt action to this end, but without avail. What is the condition of matters now ? Simply7 that we are handicapped by the United States in that market, and in addition prevented doing a coastwise trade ; that is in carrying fish to that island and having a return cargo of their products to any port in the United States which we had

hitherto enjoyed, whilst the United States is allowed all the coasting trade she desires with the British West India Islands without interruption.
Jamaica trade with Great Britain should be thought of also at the Coronation convention, in order that the bounty-fed beet root sugar of Germany, France and other countries should not be admitted into Great Britain to the exclusion of Jamaica cane-grown sugar, unless a bonus, or preference is given to Jamaica. I refer to this particularly, as our Nova Scotia trade with Jamaica is little at present, owing to their poverty stricken condition, brought about by England's free trade policy under which, in sugar, she can not compete with the bounty-fed product.
I mention this now, in the hope that the right hon. First Minister will make a note of it, and bring it forcibly to the notice of the Coronation convention meeting next month in London. Effective measures are demanded in the interest of Canadian trade, and the trade of the British Empire, I feel assured will co-equally be benefited by it.

speechtext: Oh, yes, I mav say that I was yesterday told by my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) that during mv absence on one occasion the vote had beep withdrawn.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that. The minister is quite correct in making reference to the matter.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was not properly informed on the subject. The expenditure upon this work for which we asked an appropriation this session was not for work that was done during the previous or current fiscal year, nor was it the Auditor General who made any communication to the effect that the work had not been authorized or that there had been no appropriation for it. The officer who advised the contractor, and advised him before he did any work during the last.fiscal year, was the chief engineer of the department, whose duty it was to do so. The contractor appears to have gone on with the work to a limited extent, and he has been pressing for payment, but the hon. gentleman was wrong in saying that the department recognized his claim. There is no ground whatever upon which any gentleman in the House can say that the government Intend to, or will pay for work which was done against notice and without appropriation and with the full knowledge that there was an intention on the part of the government not to continue it. This party no doubt assumed that the work would be proceeded with later, hut he assumed it without any warrant. No officer of the

government, certainly with my knowledge, held out to him any such promise, and he therefore took upon himself the entire risk of getting recouped for any work he may have done. My kon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), also made the statement that a member of this House had asserted that this work was not only useless but it was detrimental to the public interest and even injurious to navigation. The question of the Galops rapids is not by any means an easy question to determine. The work was originally started by one of the most eminent engineers who had ever been in the service of the government. I had not the pleasure of knowing Mr. Page, but there is a tradition that Mr. Page was an engineer of exceptional ability and that he was an efficient and capable officer. Mr. Page initiated this work. It was upon his strong opinion and judgment that this work was undertaken as being a necessary and proper work, and the Minister of Railways and Canals of that day agreed in Mr. Page's opinion. After Mr. Page died the work was continued under Mr. Trudeau, who is recognized as an engineer whose opinion would be entitled to very great weight, and when Mr. Rubidge took charge of the St. Lawrence canal afterwards, his judgment was in entire accord with that of Mr. Page and of Mr. Trudeau. I am afraid to say how many years Mr. Rubidge has been in the service of the government, but he has been for probably fifty years, so that he has a very lengthened experience. Mr. Rubidge has now attained the ripe age of eighty-five years. All the officers and engineers of the department who had to do with this work were of the same opinion, so that there was a continuity of approval in the department in reference to it. I am sorry that the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) is not here, but I may say that I understand that some dispute arose which led to difficulties between Mr. Rubidge and the hon. member for Grenville, and that hon. gentleman brought this subject of the Galops rapids Into parliament before I had the honour of a seat here, and he condemned the project very strongly and has continued of that opinion. 000 more will be required to complete 1 The work proceeded for three years or so in my department before any doubt was raised iat all with regard to the wisdom of continuing it. To provide for additional aids to navigation, principally on the St. Lawrence route, including the purchase of a steamer for tidal and surveying purposes, $280,000.
1 would like to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if any portion of that is contemplated to be spent on the coast of British Columbia ?

There is provision in this vote for some improvements to aids to navigation on the Pacific coast. Although the greater portion of it is intended for improvements on what is known as the St. Lawrence route, part of it is to be used in other parts of the Dominion. As the House is aware, very strong representations have been made for many years that the lighting and other aids to navigation on the St. Lawrence route are deficient. It is only necessary for me to mention, what every hon. member knows, that the larger portion of the trade of Canada is in Europe, and the object to be aimed at is to place the Canadian producer in a position to compete successfully with the exporters from other countries. To enable me to do this, I must be placed in a position to have the lowest possible charge imposed on the shipments of Canadian products to the European markets. This charge consists of two items-freight and

insurance. Ship owners have to provide for a profit on their enterprise. They have to add to the other expenses the insurance on the hull and there is also insurance on the produce to be taken into account, so that it will be seen that the high rates of insurance now charged are a heavy tax on the Canadian producers as against those of another country, who are charged lower rates. My information is that the insurance from St. Lawrence ports is from two to five times as great as from American ports. Figures given me by leading shippers of Montreal show that on a large steamer, worth say $500,000, the extra insurance charge is $5,000 per voyage, or $25,000 per season of five trips. Every one will see what a very heavy tax this is on the Canadian producer as compared with the American shipper. The reason of this high rate is undoubtedly the many casualties which have happened on the St. Lawrence route. It has been represented to us by the large shipping interests and by the marine and insurance people, that if we had very much improved aids to navigation, the rates would be reduced to those charged at American ports or at any rate would be very much reduced. I might quote from one of the official statements of the shipping interests of this country, that if the improvements recommended by them are made, the insurance rates would be very materially reduced. I have also had representations jnade to me by representatives of the largest marine insurance companies, and a representative of Lloyds, to the effect that the result would be, as I have said, to reduce the insurance very materially, if not to the same rates as are charged at American ports. Having been promised these reductions, I have come to the conclusion that it would be very much in the interests of this country to improve the aids to navigation. It must also be remembered that as our shipping season is short, lasting only during a portion of the year, we have to be particularly on the alert in competing with ports that are open all the year round, and must provide ourselves with the best facilities.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: On what principle is this money to be expended ?

I will give my hon. friend and the House a full statement of how we propose to expend these moneys. On the southern route entering the St. Lawrence the following improvements are contemplated :
Cape Race-A quick flashing light to be established and whistle changed to syren.
Cape Pine-A first-rate light and log signal to be established here, and as this is in Newfoundland, it is proposed to invite the imperial and colonial governments to co-operate with us.
Cape Ray-Improvement of light and signal.
Bird Rocks-Light to be made occulting.
Byron Island-Light to be established.
Cape Rosier-Fog alarm to be strengthened and light made occulting.
Fame Point-A syren is now being erected and light improved.
If any hon. gentleman is sufficiently interested to look at the map, which I have laid on the Table, he will see on it those points at which we propose to make these improvements.
Entering the St. Lawrence by the Strait of Belle Isle or northern route, we propose to make the following improvements :
Belle Isle-A new light and fog alarm will be placed on the north-east end.
Cape Bauld or Cape Norman-One of the fog alarms will be changed.
Point Amour-Light will be made occulting.
East End Anticosti-Lightship will be placed.
And between [DOT] the points where the two routes above mentioned join, namely, Fame Point, and Quebec, the following improvements are contemplated :
Matane-Bell buoys being placed on extremity of shoal, a syren established at station and light improved.
Father Point-A syren is being erected and the light will be improved.
Princess Shoal-This danger at the mouth of the Saguenay is being marked by a combined gas and bell buoy, which will be placed in position as soon as one can be procured.
Lower Traverse-A pier light being erected.
Belchasse-Light being made occulting.
West end of Island of Orleans-Occulting light was established at this point last autum to guide vessels on making the turn at Quebec harbour.
With regard to the route from Quebec to Montreal, I wish to state in general terms that the policy of the department is to thoroughly mark each section of the ship channel, as improved, with buoys and range lights, and changes in aids to navigation are rapidly being made.
On the 1st day of May this year, three new range lights were established at St. Antoine, to more efficiently mark a turn complained of by the pilots, and three pairs of range rights were established near Ver-eheres to mark a new channel where the Department of Public Works have done splendid work in straightening and widening an intricate reach.
The next stretch that it is proposed to improve is a dredged cat at Pointe aux Trembles.
The deepening of Lake St. Peter will be followed by a rearrangement of the lights, and the semaphore showing the depth of water over Ste. Croix Bar, where the dredging has been completed, is being moved to show the depth over St. Augustin Bar, which is now the shoalest point above Quebec.
Gas buoys are being provided for different points on the ship channel and will be placed as fast as they can be utilized.
The aim of all these improvements will be to enable a ship to run through from



Quebec to Montreal without stopping, either by day or night.
I may say that this item was under discussion yesterday, and, at the request of some hon. members, I had it stand over. But I find that these hon. gentlemen are not present. Still, I am taking the time of the committee to submit this information, because I know that it is of the greatest possible interest to those engaged in shipping. With regard to the establishment of lights in British Columbia, I intend to ask the officers of the department to visit that province at an early date, and to learn what additional aids to navigation are urgently required. The different routes to be protected are first:
The route outside Vancouver Island on the great Circle Route to Japan, principally for the safety of the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers ; second, the inside routes to Ladysmith and other coal shipping centres for the protection of the large freight steamers now engaged in carrying coal to the United States and other ports, a traffic that is rapidly increasing ; and third, the coasting trade of British Columbia, largely increased by the rapid development of lumbering, fishing and mining industries and Yukon trade in all the inlets and inside passages from the boundary line north to Fort Simpson.
Then there is the small light to be provided In Prince Edward Island, three in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick and two in the province of Quebec, on the Gasp6 coast. In Ontario, five new lights have been urgently pressed upon the department on account of the increase of trade, particularly on the Georgian Bay.
With regard to the portion of this vote to be devoted to tidal survey work, I may say that the survey of the tides and currents will be extended and it is particularly desirable that the set of the currents off Cape Pine and Cape Race should be at once investigated.
Tide tables are now prepared annually from tidal record secured by this survey for all the more important harbours in eastern Canada ; and also for the principal harbours in British Columbia. Tidal differences have also been determined, which enable the time of the tide to be known at a number of harbours of secondary importance.
An investigation of the currents was carried on during three seasons, as follows:-
1891.-In the Strait of Belle Isle and Cabot Strait; two of the entrances to the Gulf of St. Lawrence.	,
1895.-The Gaspe current and the general circulation of the currents in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
1890.-The north-eastern arm of the gulf and the steamship route from Belle Isle to Anticosti.
The regions most requiring investigation are :
(1.) Around the south-eastern coast of Newfoundland, off Cape Race and the southern bays.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
(2.) At the entrance to the Bay of Fundy.
(3.) Further investigation in several regions within the gulf, and off the outer end of Belle Isle Strait.
I am satisfied that this Improvement of the St. Lawrence route will give satisfaction to the large shipping interests especially in the old country, and that it will so meet the views of the marine insurance people that we shall get a very largely decreased rate as compared with that in force at the present time. From this comparatively small expenditure, I believe the country will reap great benefits.

In addition to the expenditure on lights, on the coast of British Columbia, I think it will be well to have a minute hydrographic survey of that coast. The steamer 'Quadra' has been doing that work spasmodically. But now that the department has two steamers to replace her, one for the lighthouse and one for the fisheries' protection service, could not the whole time of the ' Quadra ' be occupied with this hydrographic work . in future ? Her chief officer is a very competent man, who has been doing as I say, more or less of this work ever since she lias been in commission. But the great difficulty is, be has not time to do all that needs to be done. He rarely comes in without being able to add to the stock of information possessed as to the dangerous rocks on that coast. As the hon. minister knows, wrecks have been frequent on that coast since the larger vessels began navigating there. Their presence makes the need of surveys all the greater.
If I understood the hon. minister right he said he intended to devote a good deal of the grant to improving our knowledge of Newfoundland around Cape Race.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
A large part of the bad reputation under which the St. Lawrence route labours is due to the number of wrecks that have taken place in the neighbourhood of Cape Race. The marine casualties in those waters are so numerous and so unaccountable that I think it not surprising that the marine insurance companies exact high rates. If, by any reasonable expenditure, any reasonable expenditure at all, our knowledge of that locality can be enlarged so as to render impossible, or at least improbable, the occun'ence of more of the mysterious wrecks that every season occur there, it will do more to improve the reputation of the St. Lawrence route than any work that could be done within the gulf of St. Lawrence itself. The chart showing the wrecks that have occurred upon this south-eastern portion of the coast of Newfoundland must convince us that it is one of the most dangerous places for navigation in the whole world. It is not within our own waters, it

is true. But if we are to make the St. Lawrence route safe and available we must master, no matter at what cost, the knowledge of that very difficult and dangerous coast. I am glad to know that the minister has taken enough money to enable him to deal with that in a satisfactory and efficient manner. Anything short of that would be an unwise expenditure. Enough expenditure must be made in the shape of vessels and the employment of enough competent men to make that coast reasonably safe, and. if possible absolutely safe.

The particular point to which my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) refers is being covered by the British government. We have been in communication with them, and at the point where they leave oft we are taking up the work. So that, for the whole coast, we shall have the information which is so necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I hope the navigation companies will do their part and share, as we are doing our part and share. It is hardly the thing perhaps, for one minister to congratulate another publicly, but I ask to be allowed to do so iu this case. My hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has undertaken to carry out improvements that should have been carried out long ago. He is doing a most useful work for this country. But again let me ask the navigation companies not to forget that in spite of the best buoys, the best lights, the best dredged channels and other improvements, if they do not employ the right men, there will still be accidents and wrecks. It is within my personal knowledge that, in many cases our navigation companies-Canadian navigation companies as well as others-employ men who should not be engaged in such important work. They employ men who drink. For instance, I was on a ship two years ago. It was a clear day, and we were nearing Father Point, the ship struck. The captain had gone down to his room to write despatches. I had just been on the bridge, and I was glad not to have been there when the accident happened, or I might have been accused of having distracted the attention of the man who had charge of the ship. I inquired of the captain how it could be that, in full daylight, with a buoy clearly in sight, the vessel could have struck bottom. He did not tell me at the moment, but when we reached port, he said:	Well, Mr. Minister,
here are the facts : This is simply a result of false friendship; the man who was employed as my second had been commander of a steamer, but he had been drinking and was discharged, and we employed him-and here is the result of my kindness. We do our part, let the navigation companies do their part also.

The MINISTER OB' MARINE AND BTSHEK1ES. I may say that when I took charge of the department I found that representations with regard to this matter had been made iby the representatives of the marine insurance companies, by the large ship owners, and by the Board of Trade of the city of Montreal, in fact by merchants generally; and when I undertook to consider this question 1 took the reports furnished by these different bodies and asked for an interview with their leading representatives. Relief to sufferers in Martinique and St. Vinoent, $50,000.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding), it had been understood that we would have no more estimates this session, but when 1 state the purpose for which this vote is asked, 1 am sure it will have the unanimous assent of the House. We have all had our attention drawn by the press to the story of the appalling disaster which has fallen on the French island of Martinique, and to the disaster, perhaps not so great, but of a very serious character, which has fallen upon the neighbouring British island of St. Vincent. The whole world is moved to sympathy by this terrible circumstance, and there seems to be a general desire that aid should be given to those who are suffering in consequence. It is thought well that the government of Canada should contribute to this relief fund. We have therefore presented to the House an estimate appropriating the sum of $50,000 for the relief of the sufferers from the volcanic disasters in the West Indies. We propose that one-half of that sum shall be at once supplied to the relief fund for the island in which the greatest disaster has occurred, the island of Martinique; and we think that perhaps it can best be applied by placing the money at the disposal of the French colonial minister in Paris, who will, of course, be able to see that It is applied in the right direction. As respects the balance, it will, either in whole or in part, be applied for the relief of the sufferers in the island of St. Vincent. The Information respecting the disaster in St. Vincent is not yet perhaps sufficient to enable us to know whether the whole sum will be required there ; but if the necessity seems to arise, the balance will be applied to St. Vincent. At all events, the aim is that all who are suffering by these terrible disasters shall have some assistance from the government and the people of Canada In this moment of their great need.
Mr. BORDEN, (Halifax). 1 fully concur with and support the action of the government In asking parliament to make this appropriation. On occasions in the past when our own people have been in need of substantial sympathy from other countries, they have received It on many occasions in a very substantial manner. 1 think it is a fitting thing that the government should take this step at the present time. The appalling suddenness of this disaster, its tremendous extent, the amazing number of people who, in, but a moment of time, were absolutely destroyed and their homes wiped out of

I have received a communication from Halifax respecting the Bedford rifle range, and I will read a brief extract from it so that it may be brought to the attention of the Minister of Militia whom I do not see at present in the House. The letter says :
As one of a number of interested militiamen I take the liberty of writing you to ask you if you will try and get some definite answer from the Minister of Militia as to when Bedford rifle range is going to be ready for the use of the militia. Perhaps it may not be possible for you to obtain the same publicly owing to the session being so nearly to a close.
Briefly the case stands this way. A contract was awarded for the making of the new range, work being'commenced in the early fall, 1900, it being stipulated I understand that it was to be completed some time in June, 1901. Certain work done in the fall of 1900 not being properly arranged was destroyed by the spring freshets in 1901, the resuR was the militia had no range to shoot on last year and it was only through the kindness of the imperial government that the annual shooting of the provincial association was enabled to be held at Macnab's island.

The range is not ready yet and no one seems to know, when it will be, at least no one here. It looks very much as if the militia will he without any rifle practice this year as well.
A gentleman who was up viewing the range a couple of days ago, says that before the targets could even be used there is fully 1000 loads of earth that would have to be removed that had fallen into the trench from the embankment at the back, this theje would have been no trouble 'in guarding against, because it could have been foreseen, as last year they had a cave in only of a larger extent.
Entries for the ' Canadian Military League ' close on May 17th, the matches commencing June 14th, our militiamen always took an interest in these matches but owing to the uncertainty of any place to shoot there will be no entries from here, and there were none of course last year. (Barring a few individuals who formed a club and managed to shoot the matches at Macnabs with considerable expense to themselves.)
There seems to be a very strong desire on the part of this gentleman, whose name I could give to the minister if he desires, that some active measures should be taken in *order to place the range in a condition so that the militia may use Hi at the approaching season.

Porter, who resides in my province, has informed me that he has a claim against the government as to which he cannot get any reply or any satisfaction. I, Andrew E. Porter, at present of River Hebert, in the county of Cumberland and province of Nova Scotia, physician, duly admitted to the practice of medicine, do solemnly declare that :	_

air. BARKER. Before the item, is concurred in, I desire to enter my protest against charging this expenditure to capital account. I do not propose at this stage of the session, to make any extended remarks on the subject, because I have already discussed it at some length. Shortly, my objection is this-that all the hon. gentleman is really doing, in relation to a capital charge, is adding to the structure of the road 13 pounds per yard of rail. He has at present rails of 67 pounds per yard, which were originally provided out of capital. He is putting down rails weighing 80 pounds per yard. He is entitled to charge the 13 pounds of increase to capital Sir WILFRID LAURIE R.
account, but no more. That is one of the most elementary principles in companies, whether railway companies or any other. The least important business concern in the country is dealt with precisely in that way. It makes no difference whether the government own a property or whether that property is owned by a corporation, the principle is just the same. Unless you adopt a recognized principle in keeping accounts no man can tell whether the business is worked at a profit or at a loss. The importance of observing that principle was illustrated by the fact that the Minister of Finance yesterday contrasted the results obtained by the hon. Minister of Railways, as shown in his report laid before this House, with the result of the operations of his predecessors. The absurdity of such a comparison must be obvious to everybody who will consider that the predecessor of the Minister of Railways would have charged not merely the 67 pounds per yard, but the whole 80 pounds per yard to maintenance account and not to capital. By charging these rails to capital, the present minister, by this one item alone saves, as compared with his predecessors, no less than $600,000. I do not say that the hon. gentleman's predecessors were under any obligation to charge the whole SO pounds per yard to maintenance. On the contrary, I say, it would be reasonable to charge the betterment. as it is commonly called, in this instance the 13 pounds per yard, to capital. But it is absurd, and every business man in this House must see that it is absurd, when capital has provided rails of 67 pounds per yard that the hon. gentleman should replace them and charge the new ones to capital also. Why, what is the result ? You would have 67 pound rails on the road, but a charge on the books of 134 pounds. Suppose that stock was being taken of this property-that the property was being sold to some company. An accountant would be sent over to examine the property. He would find there 67 pounds of rails per yard, plus the 13 pounds, but the accounts would show a charge of 134 pounds against capital. He would naturally say : You are committing a fraud ; for your accounts represent that you have 134 pounds of rails per yard in your track, whereas you have only 67 pounds. According to the principle on which he proceeds, if the minister renews the rails again he will again charge them to capital, making the discrepancy still greater. The principle of charging to capital and to maintenance, respectively, is well understood, and, for my part, I never heard it questioned. If the hon. minister kept his accounts as any business man would keep them, he would charge to capital the betterment which he has made in the property and would charge to maintenance the replacing of the original 67 pounds of rails per yard, taking credit, against that charge to his maintenance account, for the value of the old scrap that 1 he was taking up. If that method is fol-

lowed from year to year and from administration to administration, you can compare one working with the other. But, under the system of the hon. gentleman, not only can you not compare the hon. gentleman with his predecessor, but you cannot compare two years of the hon. gentleman's own administration. I, therefore, enter my protest against this charge, as I have done before, and I desire it to be distinctly understood that, in passing this vote without dividing the House, we do not for a moment admit' the propriety of the course pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite.

Rolling stock, $500,000.

I wish to say a few words on this item, and to call the attention of the House to the question of'rolling stock. I object to this capital charge very much on the same grounds as I did with regard to the item of steel rails and fastenings. In taking up this item as the first since my remarks on steel rails, I do not wish to be understood that it is the only item upon which criticism might be offered ; because there are several items here that should call for remark. But I want to take up some special items and call attention to them. The question of rolling stock is a very large one and a very important one as regards the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railways. Hon. members will see that last year the Minister of Railways and Canals obtained authority to expend $2,000,000 upon rolling stock for the Intercolonial. In the present estimates he asks for authority to expend half a million dollars. Now the principles I refer to with regard to steel rails apply directly to the present item. The moment that a corporation, or a company, or a government, has provided for a particular work or thing upon capital account, whether it is a structure, whether it is a car, or a locomotive, or anything else, the going concern,
must thereafter maintain that which capital has once provided. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and his predecessors have received from time to time certain sums on capital account to provide rolling stock with which to operate this railroad. As a going concern the railroad is required to maintain that which capital has thus provided. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, if he maintains out of his revenue that which capital has provided, and finds that in the improvement of his business, in the increase of his business, additional rolling stock is required, he is entitled to add to his capital account whatever may be necessary to provide that additional equipment. But that is always subject to the maintenance primarily of what capital has already provided. Now, the Minister of Railways and Canals, in his last report, has shown that of his cars, provided by capital and which it was his duty, as head of the going concern, to maintain out of its revenue, 364 were condemned as unfit for the service. In addition to that, Mr. Muhlfeld, his mechanical superintendent, who was examined as a witness before the Public Accounts Committee, admitted that there were in September last from 25 to 30 locomotives which ought to be condemned, that 12 or 14 of them were already abandoned and the balance were unfit economically to be continued in the service ; and all of these 25 or 30, he said, ought to be replaced, and he admitted in his evidence that they should be replaced out of revenue and charged to maintenance.
Now, if the hon. Minister of Railways were conducting his railway as any ordinary railway company in America or anywhere throughout the world carries on business, he would before charging one dollar to capital for additional rolling stock be required to bring up to working standard the rolling stock that capital had already provided him with. If he were to replace out of maintenance these twenty-five or thirty locomotives, and to replace the 364 cars instead of allowing them to lie as he has been allowing them to lie year after year, dead and useless stock, he would not require this money on capital account. It is his business, before he asks one dollar from the country on capital account for rolling stock, to put in proper working order what he has already been provided with. I say, Sir, that before the hon. Minister of Railways is entitled to come here and ask for more stock it is his duty to show that he is already using to the full capacity what capital has provided him with ; that is to say that it is his duty to replace and put in service these 364 cars, which he admits in his report to be condemned as unfit for service, and these twenty-five or thirty locomotives, which his mechanical superintendent condemns as unfit for service. Therefore, I protest here against this authority to him to expend * $500,000 until he assumes the responsibility

of restoring the condemned stock. It is the hon. gentleman's duty, as it would be the duty of the manager of any ordinary railway, to charge the cost of replacing these cars and locomotives to his ordinary expenses. If parliament would insist upon that it would do something to protect the public against wild extravagance in the administration of government railways. I do not propose to enter into any elaborate argument upon that point. I am addressing gentlemen, who, I think, know that what I say is the ordinary rule in their own business. There are gentleman sitting upon the opposite side of this House who are connected with large corporations, and these gentlemen would not for one moment permit the officers of those corporations to charge to the capital of the company the items that are here sought to be charged to capital, but they would say to them : You must maintain that out of your revenue, and though it will add to your operating expenses you will be telling us the truth and you will enable us to know whether the concern is working at a profit or a loss. 'What would be said of a board of directors, who. year after year, allowed their management to charge to capital that which was a charge upon revenue, and thus declared a profit, or a dividend, and distributed that dividend among their shareholders though it had not been earned, when it was a fictitious dividend, when the surplus they claimed to have was really due to the fact that they were improperly charging to capital that which did not properly belong to capital ? Why, Sir, the board of directors guilty of that sort of thing would be personally responsible for their misconduct and in some countries would be severely dealt with. I protest under these circumstances against this item being made a charge to capital. Nobody, I think, from the province of Ontario desires to limit in the least degree the capacity or the usefulness of the Intercolonial Railway. We desire to see that road a success, but because we desire to see it a success we want it administered on business principles and under conditions applicable to every business organization. I repeat, that if such a manipulation of accounts as is allowed under the present administration and endorsed by hon. gentlemen opposite, were carried on in anv business concern in England, the board of directors, who in this regard have the like responsibility as the hon. gentlemen who sit as ministers in this House, would be held personally responsible for their misleading statements, for such statements as produced the so-called surplus or surpluses which have been claimed in this country during the last two or three years. It is time we should stop that sort of thing.

I should state that the Minister of Railways came over and spoke to me to-day and said that his deputy had telegraphed to Moncton for the information, but surely when the government adopts a policy in re*pect to its railways it must have decided on the extent of these improvements, and to have had before them some estimate as to the cost it was binding the country to in respect thereof.
